Working in his tunnel one day, a heavy boulder came down from the roof upon him, crushing him badly. We got him out, and carried him to his hut, but all the surgical assistance in the world couldn't have saved him. At the finish, I seas alone with him, watching for his return to coil. eciousneas. It came, but only for a few minutes; his voice was scarcely audible, as when I stooped to catch the words he strove to utter. All I could make out of them were 'under the pillow.' I gently raised it, and took from under it a wash. leather bag and a small steel chain, with a gold , locket attached. Again his eyes opened, and the I lips moved; his gaze fell upon the bag. Bending down, I caught the words, 'Pup old Crawford ' Again silence reigned for a time; then his eyes opened once more, and seeing me examining in a listless fashion the chain upon which the locket Ming, he smiled, and in a louder tone, said.

Give it to my sister, old chap ; you'll find her at--. A sudden gasp for breath, a long drawn sigh, and poor Valpy had gone from UH . . . And aowith India; the prospect in that country is improving because some portion of the load of debt and disaster has been lifted—a load which was saddled upon the people when a Tory (lovernment plunged into a wild and wicked war with Afghanistan. There is an old adage which says we should be grateful to the great that they do us no harm ; and it is on this principle, we suppose, that we are asked to praise the Tories for working less mischief than usual in foreign affairs.

Turning to matters which more immediately affect the inhabitants of this country, the Arroswav-Gassatt &WM made it clear that he had no sympathy with the struggle which the workers are everywhere making for improving I their conition. He said:—" If working-men were left free to make their own contracts and their own bargains, he dinl not think there would be much necessity for State legislation, either to , curtail the hours of lalmor, or to deal with any nif the other mattenn concerning working-men which they themselves understood much better than other people.- This is the sort of language which has always been used by the Tory party whenever an effort has been made to give the workers the benefit of just le4islation. If Snorran. PLIMSOLL himself Mut not been a brave, strong, and noble soul, he would have heen choked off with such nonsense when he set to work tin help tho British sailor in his struggle with the British shipowner. But, by a demonstration on the floor of the House of Commons, which stirred the heart of the nation, he compelled Mr. DISRAELI to listen to his de- mands, and the result was a piece of legislation which has been of great benefit. Leave the MIMICS to their own unaided efforts, and help the classes at every turn—that has for generations been the policy of the Tory party, and it is their policy tonclay ; although, now that working-men have votes, the placenbunt,rs nil the Webster type are compelled to hide it as well as they ean behind a ' cloud of "words, words, words." Passing on to refer , to Ireland, the ArronsEr-t IISNIMAL had the hardi- hood to my that tlna alliance between the Tortes end the Liberal Unionists was getting stronger , everyday; but he was pulled up by someone in the audience, who shouted, " Birmingham" and 1" Chamberlain." All he could say ins to this was that Mr. JOHN ALBERT HEIGHT WRS elected for Birmingham: hut he could scarcely have been more unfortunate if he had referred to PIGOTT ; for JOllO ALBllltfll Seat is at this moment in danger, and it is inn danger becaum the Tories, regardless of the strong alliance, are desirous of filling it with a Tory at the next election. With regard to Home Rule, Sir RICHARD plunged to the extent of saying that it VMS a imlicy which bad never been heard of before, except in order to secure Irish votes. This was intended to be a thrust at Mr. Gcanwroxs ; but is the memory of this reckless pleader so short that he has utterly forgotten how Lord CARNARVON, as the Tery Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, had interviewa with Mr. PARNIILL and discussed Home Rule with him in 15th? The ArroaNey-Gsxes. tr. boasts that Ireland has been tranquilised by Mr. BALFOUR, and that its condition has enormously improved ; but, if this he no, how is it that we hear nothing of the scheme of local self-government to which the Ministry are pledged ? Why do they not redeem their promisee? The scheme was to be similar to that for England, and it was to be sim- ultaneous. Nile' them is nothing said of the scheme ; it is relegate,' tin the crowded limbo of Tory frauds nipm the people. But it will not be allowed "fu, lie inn cold obstruction and to rot." It will be had inn mind by the Liberals when the Sir RICHARDS and Sir Gilman, are called upon to face their broken promises at the General Elec- tion.

Conghlin, O'Sullivan and Burke, the three prin- cipals who were concerned, in the United States, in the murder of Dr. Cronin, have been sentenced to penal servitude for life. There is a disposition on the part of the English press to protest against the verdict as illogical. It would seem that certain writers have already lost sight of the case of Florence Maybrick.

The Liberals of Golhorne opened new dub premises, on Saturday, under most favourable cir- curnetances. They are fortunately situated in having amongst them such a benefactor as Mr. William Mitchell, J.P. Ile has built the new club for them, and put it in their handsupon easy terms; and, as the proceedings of Saturday revealed, they are not unmindful of his kindness.

The Rector of Warrington and his curates are certainly workers. They have organised parish temperance meetings, started a nursery, and school for the blind, and now they are providing garden allotments for working-men. Those are sl works, and we wish they may bear fruit a hundredfold. The happy gardener is indeed a happy man, for there is classical authority for say- ing he can boast— retired leisure, I That in trim gardens takes his pleasure.

On Monday, a deputation from the London County Council waited upon the Home Secretary with a view to obtaining further powers to deal with the unsanitary dwellings of the poor. Mr. Matthews showed himself sympathetic and • promising, but he left no hope of performing just yet. County Councils. Town Councils, and other authorities most therefore do the hest they min and we have a strong opinion that a great deal can he done under existing Acts, if those who should enforce them are in earnest in the matter.

A case recently decided at the Manchester County Court will bring it home to farmers and others that it is an improper thing to use herbed wire as a fence on public footpaths. A Mr. Bird stepped aside to allow another person to pass hint' the barbed wire tore his coat and the County Court Judge, after hearing his tale, has allowed compensation to the amount of tb. This is good sense, and, we believe ~,orid law. The man in want of a new coat, or the woman who desires a new dress, has nothing to do but hunt out a barbed wire fence by a piddle footpath. st his, against it—accident- ally of conrse—and the thing is done.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
REPENTANCE THAT CAME TOO LATE

At the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, a woman named Mary Learns, the wife eta labourer who lives in Tilley-at., pleaded guilty to a charge of having stolen a piece of beef, of the value of a I shilling, from the shop of Thomas Bennett, butcher, Buttermarket-st. The offence was committed on Monday evening, and when Constable Monaghan taxed her with it she proferred to pay for the meat. The repentance, however, came too late. As prisoner had never been in custody before, awl as the prosecutor did not torn up, the Bench recorded a conviction and discharged Mrs. Kearns.

div.head: OUR ALMANAC ILLUSTRATION
div.p: OUR ALMANAC ILLUSTRATION

DALIIENY 110 USE AND LORD ROSEBERT. This year wsLgive an illustration of the residence, and the medallion portrait of • nobleman who, though but lightly weighted with years, has already proved himself to be a thorough statesman, and a man of brilliant paos, of whom the country and the Liberal party hopefully expect much. Dalmeny 'louse itself is a very recent structure. it was built by the late Earl of Rosebery in the midst of • richly-wooded park. in a romantic district over- looking the Firth in the county of Linlithgow. Dalroeny is a liaise of Celtic derivation, meaning a the black heath." The barony, including the lands and cast le of Barnbougle, the remains of winch are in the grounds attached to Dalmeny House, at One time belonged to the family of Mowbray, a Norman who Came Over with William the Conqueror. Philip de Mowbrav was Lord of Dalmeny is the reign of Alexander it. The barony remained in the posses-: sion of his descendants till 1615, when it was pur- chased from Sir Robt. Mowbray by Sir Thomas Hamilton, subsequently Earl of Iladdington, whose grandson in 1665 disposed of it to Sir Archibald Primrose. Bart., of Carrington, afterwards Justice- General of Scotland, and the ancestor of the prewnt Earl of Rowbery (the Right lion. Archibald Philip Primrose), who succeeded to the earldom on the death of his grandfather. the fourth Earl of Rose' hero, in 1868. It would he difficult, indeed, to find a man more personally popular than the present earl. Born, as it were, to the purple, the heir of goodly lands and a proud title, be was further favoured by fortune in Ma wedlock with one of the richest ladies in the land, who brought him not only an added material wealth. but also the priceless boon of domestic felicity. Then, from his early youth onwards. the brilliant Scottish nobleman's, innate geniality have drawn round him such a wide circle of attached admirers of all classes of society and of every mrt of thinking as few men, either in their public or private capacity, are privileged to enjoy. His life too, has been one of restless activity, physicial and intellectual. He has seen more of the world than many a man thirty or forty years his senior; and Wherever he has gone he has secured an enviable success. At an age when the public career of most Men is only in its dawning Lord Rosebery could point to a long record of work done and trust discharged. Appointed Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs by Mr. Gladstone, when only in his 39th year, he had previously held office as Lord Privy Seal, First Commissioner of Works, and Under-Secretary to the 'tome Department. Of Lord Rosebery's preferment to the Foreign Office it may safety be mud that, while it was popular with his own party, his political opponents also would rather have elected to have him at the important poet than any other statesman not of their own ranks. One of Mr. Gladstone's closest friends, Lord Rosebery Waa also on terms of personal intimacy with the Earl of Beaconsfield, who. it may be remembered, made no secret of his admiration for the gifta and accomplishments oi the young Liberal

peer-. Ilia lordship's love of literature is in part in- herited. for his father was studiously inclined, and his mother then the widowed Lady Dalmeny, but soon afterwards Duchess of Cleveland, made her mark hy the publication of such a luxurious vol- ume as has seldom felt the English press. It WU an edition de hue of that delightfully sad old metri- cal story, The Spanish Layde's Love for an Englishman," and glorious justice did the editress do to the pathetic ballad. Earl Rosebery as a boy was a special favourite for his intelligence and love of reading with his illustrious author-relative, the lord of Chevening, and many a delighted hour did young Archibald Primrose pass in the princely Stanhope library. Since then, he,like his uncle, tar tilled the Lord Rectorship chair of the University of Aberdeen, and has also held a similar appoint- ment in connection with the Edinburgh University; while he has been more latterly elected a life governor of University College, London, as a" per- son distinguished in public life:' As a speaker, Lord Roseberry is very effective having few superiors in the Lords. Ile has a com- mand of unfailing humour which serves in good stead in silencing opposing onslaughts of irony; and a scholarly earnestness which carries convic- tion and bespeaks an interested hearing even from an audience of strangers. At first sight, and espe- Melly seen from a distance,the earl has a singularly juvenile appearance, so that one would more readily conceive him to have been born in 1857, or even 1860, than in 1847; baton closer contact his lordship's clear-cut features more truthfully indi- cate his real age. Ile has, in a high degree, the courtly bearing accruing to his rank, and is, indeed, in every way well fitted to suet sin the dignities and responsibilities of statesmanship. The earl's wedding, of which we have little space to speak, WWI a most brilliant affair. It was in his 31st year that he entered the marital state. His choice had for sometime been fixed upon the present countess, and on the 21./th March, 1878, after a pre- vious civil ceremony, Lord Rosebery was united at Christ Church. Mayfair, to Hannah, only daughter, of Baron Rothschild. The Earl of Reacontiehl gave the bride away. her Majesty, the Prince of Wales, Mr. Gladstone. and hoots of others of lesser distinc- tion, joined in the felicitations. and congratulations poured in (rem friends in all parts of the world. The granddaughter of that shrewd and famous Frankforter who came to England and founded the greatest banking house in the world—who bought up at a discount Wellington's drafts on the Exchequer for the expenses of the Spanish war compelled Government to redeem them at par, and advanced at interest the money to enable them to pay him—has proved a fitting companion-helpmeet for the statesman who is the subject of this sketch.

TWO STEAMERS FOUNDERED. 13 PERSONS DROWSED.

A serious shipping disaster occurred during Thursday night off St. Catherine's Point, Isle of Wight. It is re- ported that two steamers have foundered. After the cot- Son two boat loads of men landed, but another boat with thirteen hands is missing. A dead seaman was washed ashore at Venttior, on Friday morning.

THE EXPLOSION ON THE WEAVER. On Monday a Hoard of Trade inquiry was held by Commimioners Smith and Lang, of Liverptol, at the North-Western Hotel, Winsford, attending the cinions stances connected with the explosion of the boiler on the salt steamer Development, at Salterford lock, on the I river Weaver, a few weeks since, by which tho fireman of the bat was killed. Mr. Dough was the solicitor for the Commissionem, and Mr. J. H. Cooke, of Winsford, mobbed the case for the Salt Union. In giving the de- cision of the Commissioners, Mr. Smith said they I thought that as to the specific question, no Name was ' I attached to the directors of the Union isirsonally, hot I they considered blame did attach to the company. The I Commissioners added that they considered the soperin- tendent engineer was very much to Name because he ' had seen the boiler working at a pressure which should have put hiin on his guard, and had not reported it. on this finding Mr. Hough applied for costs, and after the point had been considerably argued, the sum of E.. 45 was apportioned to be paid by the Salt Union.

div.head: ELEVEN LIVES LOH' OFF HOLYHEAD GALLANT CONDUCT.
div.p: ELEVEN LIVES LOH' OFF HOLYHEAD GALLANT CONDUCT.

On Tuesday evening a report reached Holyhead that a vessel had gone ashore near Eenrhos Head, and the life- boat wan immediately launched and the life saving apparatus sent nut, under the command of Mr. 3.0. Williams. The vessel, which went ashore at Swillies, about a inile to the south of South Stack, was found to he the 'renbv Castle, Captain Davies, from St. Namire to Barrow, in &sliest. She struck on the nicks and broke amidships. Eleven of the crew were drowned, and three were saved by a local boat. Those saved were foreigners. It wus a little south to the place that the Missouri struck three and a half years ago. A cornispondent, describing the wreck, refers to the gallant conduct of William Owen, pilot, Holyhead Geore,e Jones, en-lifeboat man; and John Morris, of Olangormoch, fanner, who, finding that the lifeboat could not be summoned in time, launched a small boat , in the darkneas, and pulling through the surf saved three men. The rtsnainder of the crew—eleven—refused to jump into the ma to the boat, and wore drowned.

div.p: DARESBURT HIGHWAY BOARD.

A special meeting of this Hoard was held on Thursday afternoon, for the purpose of considering several matters affecting the roads in the district. Mr. Edward lireenall presided, and there were also present Meson. W. Long, J. Cliffe, E. Clarke, T. G. Higby, W. Bradford, W. 'Fickle, J. 1.. Jones, Peter Tickle, J. Darbyshire, T. S. Burgess, It'. THE ROADS AND THE SHIP CANAL. The Clerk said the Manchester Ship Canal Company had deposited plans for their new works, more especially as regarded the alterations in the Board's distract. Ile would suggest that a Committee be appointed to instruct the Clerk to get a copy of the Bill, and carefully to go through thew clauses affecting the district—The suggestion was agreed to on the proposition of Mr. Chile, seconded by Mr. Rigby. The Clerk further reported that plans had been depositnl by the Widnes Brine supply Company, who proposed to cut up 114 miles of the Board's roads to lay moist—lt was decided to refer the matter to the Roads Committee.

The Clerk nod the minutos of the Ship Canal Com- mittee with reference to the road at Walton. A meeting of the Committee was heldon the 12th Dm:ember, when they inspected the roads leading from Walton to War- rington by way of Arpley meadows. The road was macadamisl 25 feet wide. After some discussion it was decided that the Company be required to make the road 30 feet in width. The minutes were confirmed. . . _ .

The minutes of a meeting of the Ship Canal Com- mittee, on the 23rd November, were also read. At the meeting Mr. Walker made application to stop up Knutsford-rd., and direct the traffic by the new road on to the Grappenhall-rd.. and across a temporary bridge into Warrington. After a long diemssion, it was de- cided that permission be granted, subject to the approval of the county surveyor, to close the road on the Ist January, that the Grappenall-rd. be made 5 feet wider, and that the temporary bridge be left intact until the permanent bridge was ready.—The Clerk thought the contractor should maintain the new road until the County Council took it over.—Mr. Long dissented from the action of the Committee, because lie thought it would be time enough to close the road two rearm hence. At the Committee meeting Mr. J. Walker admittedthat they could not complete the Knutsford-road for another 18 months or two years, on account of the construction of the London and North-Western Itailway.—The Clerk said he had received a notice from the County Council saying that they were going to take over the new road on the lot of April—After some discussion, the minutes were rescinded, as it was stated that it was of no use proceed- ing in the matter, as the County Council were dealing with the matter. This was all the business.

div.head: MANCHESTER AND LIVERPOOL AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.
div.p: MANCHESTER AND LIVERPOOL AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.

The annual meeting of the Manchester, Liver- pool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society was held yesterday morning, at the Lion Hotel, Warrington, in order to receive the annual report, elect officers, and transact other yearly business. The chair was taken by Mr. G. C. Hale, of Liverpool, and there was a large attendance of members. The annual report of the Council stated that the chow held this year at Wigan had resulted in an improvement of the financial state of the Society. Nearly £2,000 was received for admission, and .1:000 was contributed by the local Committee. The society had distributed £1,533 lila. in prizes for farms, and for farm stock and implements; had paid nearly E. 101) for technical instruction and illustra- tion an the show yard, and had continued the prac- tical teachings of its experimental fields in the cultivation of the potato, in laying down land to grass, the making of the best pasture land, and in the methods of manuring grass land for inowing. It was gratifying to the Council to report that this had been effected,and that the funds of the society had been increased by £370 155.7 d. The general balance in favour of the society last year was £240 B.s. liii It now stood , at £Bll 4s. eid. It had been arranged that the next show be bald at Crewe. The Cheshire County Agricultural society gave up holding its show in 1880. and co-oper- ated with that Society in realising a large and useful exhibition. Already a sub-committee of the two societies had met and arranged a price list upon which , they thought the amalgamation might be again effectsl. The ChishireSociety were to contribute the sum of £250. in consideration of which the Society tattle provisions as to entmnee of members of the Cheshire Society, and engaged to offer a prise list of £1,500. At the sugges- tion of the Cheshire Agricultural Society prizes were proissel for labourers cottage gardens, and for general management. The demand for well-bred horses to go abroad. and for pedigree shins and Clydesdale horses. especially confirmed the wisdom of offering literal prises for breeding horses of registered pedigree. The Council proposed that the sum of £1,500 he fiXPil upon for allotment in prism for the show-yard, £lOO prises for farms and cottages, and that a stun net ex- ceeding £lOO be expended on the experimental fields.t he working dairy, and the horse-shoeing conipetition. Mr. Rigby. secretary fir twenty years, desired to resign. tot at the request of the Council consented to remain in office until after the next show.—The Chairman, in pro- posing the adoption of the report, said that the WM, tary had bmueht the society to a very high position amongst agriculturists, and his severance from the society would be Very muell regretted—Mr. It. Lans- dale areonded the proposition, and speaking of the finan- cial position of the society, said he thinight that at Past £l,OOO should be received in subscriptions.— After further discussion, the report and tsdance sheet were adopted.-1 In the proposition of Mr. John White (Warrington), seconded by Mr. T. Egerton Tatton Wytldinshawis, it resolution was adoptel thanking th Mayor and Corporation of Wigan for the support given to the society on the occasion of tbe last show, held at that town.—Mr.Scotson (Aigborthl, proposed, and it was resolved, that the nist year's show be held at Crewe.on the 24th, 25th, and 26th days of July, I69o.—The following gentlisnen were nominated for the position of president Mule society for next year —herd Crew', Colon./ Cotton, M.P., Sir Richard Wilbraham, and Sir Philip Egerton.—The meeting then proceeded to the plectien of members of the Council, and afterwards luncheon was served.

It was to the local authorities they must look for providing schools where higher education could be obtained at a reasonable price, and thun help their countrymen in competition with foreign nations to gain their daily bread. (Applause.)—Mr. Carey seconded the proposition, and said the report of the Committee I gave a eery strong hint to the Local Board, and they told Diem in a very few words what the Local Board ought to do in regard to technical Mum- 1 tion. miasmas - TIDE AT WARRINGTON. -- Warrington yesterday began to put on Christmas garb. Many of the shopkeepers of the town are very busily engaged decking out their establish- ments in the most attractive manner possible, and some of them haying already completed the work, have made a grand show for the admiring gam of the public. Chief among these are the poulterers, whose shops were last evening surrounded by crowds of sightseers. The butchers, too, made a very credit- able exhibition, and their places of business came in for a large share of the attention of heads of families, who are contemplating a seasonable expend it ore of money on the good things that ore no plentiful at the Christmas festival. Some of the fruiterers in the market have also already dis- played their tempting stock, and others are in the thick of preparations for to-day, when, it may be expected, the market will be a scene of a bright and festive kind. Not to be left behind, tradesmen whose businesses are of all sorts and conditions are making ready, and they expect to do a big trade between now and Christmas Day. Next week we shall be in a position to go more into detail with regard to the " Christmas Show." We may add that Nlessrs. Woods and Sons, jewellers, Sankey-st., are present- ing their customers with a most artistic calendar. I in gold and green, the unique feature of which is a small thermometer and centrepiece. div.p: 'STONE THROWING AT BUItTONA-0411
A SMALL RIOT."

At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Colonel George McCorquodale and Messrs. T. J. Gillespie, A. C. McC3rquala/e, T. D. Orimke, and W. Mitchell. nine youths named Schofield, Jackson, Charles Jackson, Thomas Haverty, James Haverty, Henry Dalton, James Dalton. Joseph Dalton, Jame. Millington, and Earnest Naylor. were summoned for having aseaulted Thomas Dutton, a wheelwright by throwing stones at him, at Burtonwood, on the 17th ult. There was • crons-summone against Dut- ton, charging him with having assaulted the boys Joseph Dalton and Naylor, at the same time.—Mr. H. L. Riley, of St. Helens, appeared for Dutton. and the lads were represented by Mr. W. 11. Jenkins, of Warrington, who stated that he appeared in the place of Mr. P. Davies, solicitor, who had been in- structed and who was unable to attend through serious illness.

• Mr. Itileystated that his client had for something liken • quarter of a century carried on business and had been a • reputable inhabitant of Buttonwood. Unfortunately as it • had turned out,he had been a witness at that court upon , oceasions when boys had been chargedand onthataccount had berme obnoxious to the young of Burtonwood • The boys, on the 17th ult., appeared to have organised something of the nature of a small riot directed against ' Mn. Dutton. On that night he had occasion to go to . Collin's Green station,and he had with him a small terrier • , dog. On the any Ire was met by the defendants who , called tollim rhytningquestionsan whielo the final syllabi.. rhymed with Dutton, and when he had passed them they threw stones at him and his dog. They follnwed him to the station, and there a piece of gla.ss was thrown at him . while he was sitting on a form. On leaving the station ! he was met by the lads, who again attacked him. Senn.. ! , one shouted out "fire,' he is," and he 1 ad to return to the , • station. Ho was followed, and he seized Henry Dalton, I who, in the presence of the booking-clerk, gave the ' names of the defendants as having been with him. When he finally left the station in company with the booking- ' clerk the stone-throwing was cnntinued and the elerk received a blow on the leg from one of the stones.— Thomas Dutton. the complainant, then gave evidence. .Froin first to last he never did anything to irritate the lads.— In roply to Mr. Jenkins complainant said he was not in the habit of threatening the boys and he had never chased them with his sticks—Henry Singleton, the honking clerk at Collins Green station, gave corrobora- tive eridenve—D illium Hewitt, a boy, gave evidence that fare f the defendants had used threats concerning the tiomplainent.—Mr. Jenkins, for the defence, con- tended that no assault had been proved, because there was trot a tittle of evidence to identify any of the defendants as having thrown a stone.—He called an wit. neves James lion»Ii•v, ; John Doran, check. weightnan. and John Williams, collier, all of whoin rind they saw the do.fendants and Mr. Dutton on the night in question. They did not see any stones thrown. The cross summons against Dutton was then heard. It was alleged that Dugan attempted to strike the boys named with his stick, and that he at las donut them. After Rover,' witnesses had given their evidence, the Bench retired. After five minutes' absence they re- turned. and the Chairman said each of the boys would he fined ss. and costs, and the ease against limber would be diamissed. The Chairman said he would like to point nut to the superintendents that stone-throwing by boys was not confined to Burtonwood, or to the neighbourhood of the Pear Tree ; and the 'tench would like instructions to be given for all offenders to be brought before them.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL, CORRESPONDS/QT.

The wants of Widnes are not a few, but in many respects the town is in advance of its neighbours and scarcely merits the title of " the black spot on, the Mersey," by which it is known to many. At the meeting of the Science and Art Schools, on Monday evening, Mr. Gossage mentioned a few ot the advantages the townspeople possessed, in an educational sense, and Illeffied his approval of the establishment of a Technical School by the Local Board, which the committee of the Science School advocated in their report. Dr. Hurter and Mr. Carey also spoke strongly in favour of such a school, and the project being engineered by those warm well wishes of the people, it is safe to predict that the desired object will be attained. Of course the rates would be increased to a certain extent if a technical school were firmed, but, compartsl with the rates of other towns of similar size, they are very low at present, whilst gas and water is sold nn an exceedingly cheap scale. In no town iu the kingdom is a scientific education snore needed for those wino take part in local industries, and a Technical School would be both a boon and a blessing. The Widnes Board Schools continue (0 maintain their character as well managed and highly successful astab- lishments, as a glance at the repoit of the monthly meeting of the Board on Tuesday will show. If in one department there Is a slight reduction in the per eentage of passes, and the grant earned, it is more than compen- sated for by an increase in another department, and Ova total result cannot be other than gratifying to those interested in education. The average grant earned per head in the schools is is. 54d. more than the average throughout the country, a fact which speaks for itself without comment.

In the course of a few days the chief festival of the Christian Church will be celebrated, and it is pleasing to record that the majority of the inhabitants of the twin towns of the Mersey will be able to enter into the joyous festivities of the season, unburdened by any de- pressing external circumstances. Work is plentiful, wages are good, and the weather, not being of the kind called •sseasonable,” but warm and open, is a distinct advantage to those upon whom the hand of poverty is heavily laid. May all have a Merry Christmas is the wish of Occasional Correspondent." Runcorn Musical Society are to be congratulated on the success which attended their performance of the Messiah, on Tuesday last. In one's peregrinations through the town, only the most unqualified praise of those who took iiart is heard, and the energetic and able conductor, Mr. E. Wynne Humphries, is the subject of the wannest eulogies for the pitch of perfection to which he had trained the numerous band of choristers. The next oincert of the society will be awaited with been interest.

_ OVERTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL —The annual entertain- ment by the scholars was held in the above school Last evening week, when the Vicar, the Rev. If. B. Blogg, MA., presided. The pmgramme consisted of songs, choruses, recitations, and dialogues, given entirely by those connected with the school, under the superintend- ence of Mr. Hutton, the assistant master. There was such a nutnerous attendance of parents and friends that seats could not be provided for all. At the close of the programme the Chairman called for a hearty cheer for Mr. Pollard, head master, and also one for Mr. Hutton, assistant master, the labour in getting up the programme having devolved chiefly upon him. Ilearty charm were also accorded to Masters P. Earlam pertain pianist), P. Robinson, and R. Foulkes, and Messrs. E. Tear and bwarbrick, for their respective servitaw.

div.head: 4THERTDN MURDER.
div.p: THE 4THERTDN MURDER.

At Leigh, yesterday, William Chadwick was again charged with the murder ,d Walter Davies, at Atherton, on the 22nd July last.—Witnesses were called for the purpom of identifying deceased's watch and chain.— John Lowe, pawnbroker, of Atherton, identified some clothing and jewellery, missed from his shop alter the murder, and deposed to finding the deceased in the cel- lar, cut about tho body and with wounds in the head. The court adjourned for an hour until two o'clock, after which the first witness called was Dr. Sephton, who spoke to the situation of the body in the cellar and to the nature of the injurim.—Janies Roylance, milkman, living in High-at., Atherton, said he knew the prisoner, and about a fortnight before the murder he saw him in Market-nt., Atherton.—James Itidyard, fireman, mid that on the morning of the murder, while standing at his own door in Leigh-road, Atherton, he saw the prisoner. He next saw the prisoner at Strangeways Gaol last Saturday. There was a lot of them exoreising, marching round a ring, and he picked the prisoner out. He had no doubt stall the prisoner woo the man he saw on the day of the murder. The case was adjourned, there being about 40 witnesses. The murdered man was a native of Widnes.
